Where the deadlock really comes from
needs a context that runs one thing at a time, such as a UI thread, plus code that blocks it. The UI thread calls
on a library method and waits. Inside the library, an
finishes and queues the rest of the method back to the UI thread. The UI thread is busy waiting for that very method, so neither side moves.

in the library breaks the cycle, because the library no longer needs the UI thread to finish. But the root cause is the blocking call. Awaiting instead of blocking removes the deadlock no matter what the library does.

A general-purpose library, such as a NuGet package or an SDK shared by several apps, can't know who calls it. Its code doesn't need any particular thread, and posting continuations back to a busy UI thread costs time and risks the deadlock above. So libraries should use

. Application code is the opposite: UI event handlers and view models need to come back to the UI thread to update controls, which is why the context exists. In app code, the FAQ's advice is plain: don't use it.

How to apply it in your project
Mark every project as application code or as a general-purpose library. The answer decides the rule; the platform alone doesn't.
